q.t: The distance from the centre of a circle to any point on it is called the:
q.e: Every point of a circle is the same distance — the radius — from the centre.

q.t: A circle has radius 5 cm. Find its diameter (in cm).
q.e: A diameter goes right across through the centre: two radii end to end.

q.t: A line segment joining any two points on a circle is called a:
q.e: A chord joins two points of the circle; it need not pass through the centre.

q.t: The longest chord of a circle is its:
q.e: A chord is longest when it passes through the centre.

q.t: A circle has diameter 14 cm. Find its radius (in cm).
q.e: The radius is half the diameter.

q.t: The length of the boundary of a circle is called its:
q.e: It is the circle’s perimeter.

q.t: All the radii of one circle are:
q.e: That is what makes it a circle: every point is equally far from the centre.

q.t: A part of the circumference of a circle is called:
q.e: An arc is a curved piece of the circle itself.

q.t: Half of a circle is called a:
q.e: ‘Semi’ means half. A diameter cuts a circle into two semicircles.

q.t: The fixed point in the middle of a circle is its:
q.e: The compass needle stands at the centre while the pencil draws the circle.

q.t: A circle has radius 3.5 cm. Find its diameter (in cm).
q.e: Diameter = 2 × radius.

q.t: How many radii can a circle have?
q.e: One to every point on the circle.

q.t: How many diameters can a circle have?
q.e: One in every direction through the centre.

q.t: A circle has diameter 9 cm. Find its radius (in cm).
q.e: Half of 9.

q.t: The region between two radii and the arc joining them is called a:
q.e: A sector is shaped like a slice of pizza.

q.t: The region between a chord and its arc is called a:
q.e: A chord cuts the circle’s inside into two segments.

q.t: Circles with the same centre but different radii are called:
q.e: ‘Con-centric’ means sharing a centre, like ripples in a pond.

q.t: A point is 6 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. The point lies:
q.e: It is further from the centre than the radius.

q.t: A chord that passes through the centre is a:
q.e: It is the longest possible chord.

q.t: A quarter of a circle has an angle at the centre of:
q.e: A quarter of the full turn of 360°.

q.t: Two circles of radii 5 cm and 3 cm touch each other from outside. How far apart are their centres (in cm)?
q.e: The centres and the touching point lie in a line: one radius plus the other.

q.t: A circle of radius 3 cm touches a circle of radius 5 cm from the inside. How far apart are their centres (in cm)?
q.e: The small circle sits inside against the edge: 5 − 3.

q.t: What is the longest chord of a circle of radius 6.5 cm (in cm)?
q.e: The longest chord is the diameter.

q.t: Two concentric circles have radii 7 cm and 4 cm. How wide is the ring between them (in cm)?
q.e: The ring’s width is the difference of the radii.

q.t: A point is 3 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. The point lies:
q.e: It is closer to the centre than the radius.

q.t: The diameter of a circle is 6 cm more than its radius. Find the radius (in cm).
q.e: Diameter = 2r, so 2r = r + 6 and r = 6.

q.t: A line that touches a circle at exactly one point is called a:
q.e: A tangent just brushes the circle.

q.t: A line that cuts a circle at two points is called a:
q.e: The part of a secant inside the circle is a chord.

q.t: The perimeter of a semicircular plate is made of:
o: Half the circumference and a diameter
q.e: The curved edge plus the straight edge.

q.t: A regular hexagon is drawn inside a circle of radius 4 cm with all its corners on the circle. Find the length of each side (in cm).
q.e: Joining the centre to the corners makes six equilateral triangles, so each side equals the radius.

q.t: Three circles of radius 2 cm each touch the other two. Find the perimeter of the triangle formed by joining their centres (in cm).
q.e: Each pair of centres is 2 + 2 = 4 cm apart, giving an equilateral triangle of side 4 cm.

q.t: The largest possible circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 cm. Find its radius (in cm).
q.e: The circle’s diameter equals the side of the square.

q.t: Two concentric circles have diameters 20 cm and 12 cm. Find the width of the ring between them (in cm).
q.e: Use the radii: 10 − 6 = 4. (Not 20 − 12.)

q.t: Five points are marked on a circle. How many chords can be drawn joining them in pairs?
q.e: One chord for each pair of points: 5 × 4 ÷ 2.

q.t: Three equal circles of radius 3 cm are placed in a straight row, each touching the next. Find the total length of the row (in cm).
q.e: Three diameters end to end: 3 × 6.

q.t: What is the diameter of the largest circle that fits inside a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm (in cm)?
q.e: The circle is limited by the shorter side.

q.t: A circle has diameter 17 cm. How far is any point on the circle from the centre (in cm)?
q.e: That distance is the radius, half the diameter.

q.t: Two circles of radii 7 cm and 4 cm cross each other at two points. Which could be the distance between their centres?
q.e: They cross when the distance is between 7 − 4 = 3 and 7 + 4 = 11. At exactly 3 or 11 they only touch.

q.t: A circle is divided into 8 equal sectors. Find the angle at the centre of each (in degrees).
A chord of a circle is as long as its radius. The triangle formed by the chord and the two radii to its ends is:
q.e: All three sides equal the radius.
